solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What may contain mild defect, nothing more for Spooner?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so this asks for that swap

parts.note: mere = nothing more; it takes the B from the other word
a bug is a defect; it takes the M from the other word

explanation.surface: Someone describes a trivial flaw and asks how Spooner would put it.
explanation.walkthrough: Mild is a dark, low-strength British beer, so the definition is a container for it, not a gentle remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: mild is a beer, and this is the vessel a pint of it is drunk from.

clue.text: Pardon received by supreme order

indicators.note: one thing received by another is taken inside it

explanation.surface: A pardon granted on the highest authority.
explanation.walkthrough: "Supreme order" reads as one phrase, but the break comes after "supreme".
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly formal: something done at someone's bidding is done on their command.

clue.text: I will shackle introduction of merchandise but not stop trade

indicators.note: the introduction of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the ego is the I, the self

explanation.surface: A trader vows to restrain new goods without halting business altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: "I will" reads as a promise, but I is the ego and "will shackle" is the container. The definition is a verb phrase, so the answer is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb for a government ban: to prohibit commerce with a country is to impose this.

clue.text: Possibly unable to start a fire without peer

definitions.text: Possibly unable to start a fire
definitions.meaning: a fire-lighter who has run out of the little sticks you strike

explanation.surface: A would-be fire-starter, stuck without a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a whimsical reading of the word as match + less; "Possibly" flags that it is not a dictionary meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: having no equal, and literally lacking a match to strike.

clue.text: See red mug on ledge upset after a jerk

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down, reading it bottom to top

parts.note: gob and mug are both slang for the mouth or face

indicators.note: the reversed ledge comes after A

parts.note: a window ledge is a sill
a tic is an involuntary jerk

explanation.surface: Someone knocks a mug off a ledge after a sudden twitch and loses their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface mug is a cup falling off a shelf; here it is slang for the mouth. In a down clue "on" means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for sudden rage, like a missile launching; seeing red is losing your temper.

clue.text: Not fed on bananas very much

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters go mad

explanation.surface: A remark that someone was not fed on bananas very much as a child.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bananas" looks like the food in the diet; it is the instruction to rearrange FED ON.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for a limitless amount: "it helped no end" means it helped a great deal.

clue.text: Once called for a woman, or rather for somebody who listens

indicators.note: the second meaning only works for a listener, since the word is said like NAY

parts.note: the French word for born, placed before a married woman's former name
nay = or rather, as in "good, nay, excellent"

explanation.surface: Once a word used of a woman, now one for a listener.
explanation.walkthrough: Née is French for born and precedes a woman's maiden name; it is pronounced like nay.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: the marker of a woman's maiden name, and a sound-alike of nay, meaning or rather.

clue.text: Lopped branch remains after incineration

indicators.note: lopping cuts off the top, here the first letter

parts.note: a branch of an organisation is a member; a limb is also a member

explanation.surface: A cut branch leaves only ashes once burnt.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a lopped tree branch on a bonfire; the branch is a MEMBER, a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a glowing coal is what is left once a fire has burnt down.

clue.text: Feature of knitted — but not crocheted — garment

definitions.text: Feature of knitted — but not crocheted —
definitions.meaning: look at the spelling: kniTTed has two of one letter, croche-Ted only one

explanation.surface: A garment made by knitting rather than crochet.
explanation.walkthrough: The feature is in the spelling, not the fabric: knitted has a double T.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a man's close-fitting Tudor jacket, and a double T read as two words.

clue.text: Female soldiers plough Clarkson's land?

parts.note: an ard is a primitive plough

explanation.surface: Women soldiers ploughing the fields of a TV presenter's farm.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Clarkson, the car-show presenter, now runs a farm in a TV series, hence the question mark. ARD is an old scratch plough.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Clarkson's Farm is his TV show, so his land is the yard around a farm.

clue.text: OK to occupy hotel (not much food when sharing a cell)

indicators.note: the two pieces overlap in one grid square, sharing the T

parts.note: H is Hotel in the phonetic alphabet
TABLE (food, as in "keeps a good table") with its T shared with A BIT

explanation.surface: A prisoner complains the hotel-like cell is fine but the rations are meagre.
explanation.walkthrough: A BIT and TABLE overlap on one T, one crossword cell, so the grid holds A BI(T)ABLE; "cell" is the prison joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a building fit to live in is OK to occupy.

clue.text: Further to the right, further down

definitions.meaning: blue is the colour of the UK Conservative party

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain blue is the Conservative colour, so bluer is more right-wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: more Tory in politics, and sadder in mood.

clue.text: What's laid back and unfeeling taking diamonds off retired woman

indicators.note: laid back = turned backwards

parts.note: as = what, as in "do as I say"

indicators.note: retired = gone back, so reversed

explanation.surface: A relaxed, hard-hearted person stripping jewels from an elderly lady.
explanation.walkthrough: "Laid back" and "retired" look like descriptions of people; both are reversal instructions, one for AS and one for HAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: any woman's first name will do, and this is a common one.

clue.text: Injury-time recovery from one's side?

parts.note: injury time is added at the end of a match

explanation.surface: A team pulls back a late goal in stoppage time.
explanation.walkthrough: "One's side" reads as a football team; the definition is the sideways direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sideways, coming from the flank rather than head-on.

clue.text: Antiques got smashed, didn't they?

indicators.note: smashed pieces are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks for confirmation that the antiques were broken.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an example: "didn't they?" is itself a tag question, tacked onto the statement before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: "didn't they?" is a short question tacked onto a statement.

clue.text: One badly wants to keep butterfly enclosure

indicators.note: one word keeps the other inside it

parts.note: the ringlet is a brown butterfly

explanation.surface: A collector craving a butterfly house.
explanation.walkthrough: "Enclosure" suggests a pen for the butterfly; it is something enclosed in an envelope.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the letter sent with a CV is enclosed in the envelope, so it is an enclosure.

clue.text: Testing start for Antonelli, opening out of the pits?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: ex = out of; pits are mines, so mining

indicators.note: A opens up EX-MINING, splitting it

explanation.surface: A Formula One driver's trial run as he leaves the pit lane.
explanation.walkthrough: Kimi Antonelli is a Formula One driver, and the pits sound like the pit lane; here they are coal mines.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: inspecting or quizzing someone, as in an exam.

clue.text: Waiving fine, FA reportedly suspended City

indicators.note: waiving the F means doing without it
a report is something said and heard, so the word is taken by its sound

explanation.surface: The Football Association lets a fine go and suspends a club called City.
explanation.walkthrough: FA and City look like football, the Football Association and a club; FA is just letters, and City is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the capital of South Australia.

clue.text: Edge of pound coin assigned this, originally Latin as agreed?

definitions.text: Edge of pound coin assigned this, originally Latin as agreed?

parts.words: Edge of pound coin assigned this
parts.note: the surface pushes a design detail; the setter means the words inscribed around the rim of the British pound
reads as a committee's decision; it hints that the phrase is Latin and sounds like a formal phrase meaning as agreed

explanation.surface: A committee agreed a Latin inscription for the rim of the pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: The motto, meaning "an ornament and a safeguard", was put on coin edges to deter clipping; "as agreed" plays on it sounding like official Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin motto lettered on the rim of British pound coins, meaning an ornament and a safeguard.

clue.text: A delicacy one's served as a result of being in charge

indicators.note: the piece before it is placed in, inside, the word that follows

parts.note: in someone's charge = in their care

explanation.surface: A person in charge is served caviar as a perk.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an older spelling of caviar.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: sturgeon roe, the classic luxury food served to guests.

clue.text: Wearing down hare, say, tortoise finally leads

indicators.note: the final letter of tortoise
to lead is to go in front, so the letter comes first

parts.note: "say" admits the hare is only loosely a rodent

explanation.surface: In the fable, the tortoise wears down the hare and takes the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: The tortoise-and-hare fable is decoration; "say" covers the fact that a hare is not strictly a rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, rare: an adjective for what erodes, gnawing slowly away.

clue.text: Spent summer in St Tropez supporting blind partner?

indicators.note: in a down clue, the supporting word sits underneath

parts.note: "effing and blinding" pairs the two ways of swearing

explanation.surface: A holiday romance in St Tropez with someone who cannot see.
explanation.walkthrough: "Effing and blinding" is British for swearing, so eff is the partner of blind. "Spent" looks like past tense of spend; here it means exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: worn out, having lost vigour, as a spent force has.

clue.text: Numbers following it, odd cult is minding one's back

indicators.note: odd means strange, so the letters are rearranged
CULT IS minds, keeps, the other piece inside
the piece is read backwards

parts.note: anagram fodder, split around the next piece

explanation.surface: An odd cult watches its members' backs.
explanation.walkthrough: Numbers is the book of the Bible that follows this one, so "Numbers following it" defines it; it is not a count.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by position: the third book of the Old Testament, with Numbers coming right after.

clue.text: It's criminal taking a newspaper

definitions.meaning: the pink British business daily, known by its initials with the article in front

explanation.surface: Pinching someone's newspaper is a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as THE FT: the Financial Times is a British newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: the crime of stealing, and the Financial Times split into two words.

clue.text: Foul now, unfit for consumption

explanation.surface: Food that has turned rotten and inedible.
explanation.walkthrough: "Foul" reads as rotten; it is the snooker foul where the cue ball goes into a pocket after hitting another ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A snooker and billiards term: potting the cue ball off another ball, which is a foul.

clue.text: How house and home end up empty?

parts.note: answer the question how they end: in a certain letter, preceded by the article

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of both words

explanation.surface: A question about why a house and home end up bare.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer the question literally: house and home both end IN AN E.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: vacuous, empty of sense or content.

clue.text: A right puritan disturbed by very bad English

parts.note: a prig is a self-righteous prude

explanation.surface: A puritan upset by dreadful English.
explanation.walkthrough: "A right puritan" reads as a real prude; "A right" is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a special entitlement or advantage granted to some.

clue.text: Vegetable, like any other, going individually for a song, it seems

parts.note: p = penny, a price as cheap as a song
surface padding: admits the price is only a pretence

explanation.surface: A vegetable sold cheaply, one at a time, like any other.
explanation.walkthrough: Any vegetable could be priced "1p ea" (a penny each), which is why the clue says "like any other" and "it seems".
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the small green seed of a pod, as ordinary a vegetable as any.

clue.text: Complex figure destined to take position beside God

parts.note: as in president-elect, destined for office

explanation.surface: A chosen one about to be seated at God's side.
explanation.walkthrough: "Complex figure" is a figure with a psychological complex named after her, not a complicated shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: the Greek heroine who gave her name to a daughter's complex in psychoanalysis.

clue.text: Change of ends for rowing crew in late shift

indicators.note: the first and last letters trade places

parts.note: an eight is a rowing crew

explanation.surface: A rowing crew swaps ends of the boat during a late training session.
explanation.walkthrough: EIGHT IN with its outer E and N swapped. "Late shift" suggests work hours; a shift is also a loose dress.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on shift: a loose nightdress is a shift worn late at night.
